title: Positioned for a Rally: 5 Reasons Stocks Could Soar into Year-End
detail:
Positioned for a Rally: 5 Reasons Stocks Could Soar into Year-End
Ethan Feller
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 11:27 AM MST 14 min read
^NDX
CL=F

The stock market has endured a difficult stretch these last few weeks, with the Nasdaq 100 suffering a sharp correction and selling pressure spreading across growth stocks and other economically sensitive areas.

But zooming out, the frustration has been building for months. Despite strong year-to-date returns, the major indexes have made relatively little sustained progress since early summer, as a growing list of concerns has weighed on investor sentiment.

Rising interest rates, persistent conflict in the Middle East, elevated oil prices, tighter Federal Reserve policy and renewed questions surrounding the sustainability of the AI boom have all contributed to an increasingly uncertain environment.

However, I believe the market may be approaching an important turning point.

For much of this bull market, I have argued that two powerful forces have been driving equities higher: the historic AI capital expenditure boom and persistent fiscal deficit spending. 

AI infrastructure investment is generating extraordinary revenue and earnings growth across semiconductors, memory, networking, power generation and a rapidly expanding ecosystem of related industries. Meanwhile, substantial government deficit spending continues to support nominal economic growth and corporate revenues, even as it creates longer-term fiscal challenges.

Neither of these underlying forces have disappeared. Rather, their positive influence has recently been overshadowed by a series of bearish macroeconomic developments.

And that is what makes the current setup particularly interesting.

With valuations improving, corporate earnings remaining exceptionally strong and several potential catalysts approaching, I believe the recent correction could prove to be the foundation for a powerful rally into year-end and early 2027.

Here are five reasons why. 

1) Stock Market Valuations Have Reset 

One of the most encouraging developments has been the improvement in equity valuations.

While stock prices have struggled in recent months, corporate earnings and forward estimates have continued climbing. That combination has produced meaningful valuation compression, particularly across the leading sectors.

This is an important distinction. A market doesn't necessarily need to experience a major bear market to become more attractively valued. Extended periods of sideways price action can accomplish much the same thing, provided earnings continue growing. And that is largely what has happened.

The Nasdaq-100, for example, now trades around 20 times forward earnings, compared with its 10-year median of approximately 23 times. That represents a notable discount to its historical valuation, despite the index's substantial exposure to some of the world's fastest growing and most profitable companies.

Of course, not everything is cheap. Some AI infrastructure businesses still command substantial premiums, and elevated Treasury yields make those valuations more difficult to justify. But the broader opportunity has clearly improved.

Many high-quality companies are now trading at substantially more reasonable multiples than they were earlier this year, even as analysts have continued raising earnings expectations.

Should interest rates stabilize and investor sentiment improve, those companies could benefit from both continued earnings growth and renewed valuation expansion. 

2) Corporate Earnings Are Booming and Could Broaden Significantly 

Perhaps the strongest argument for the bull market is the remarkable resilience of corporate earnings.

According to the latest Zacks estimates, S&P 500 earnings are expected to increase +24.6% year over year in the third quarter, supported by +11.8% revenue growth. That would mark the eighth consecutive quarter of double-digit earnings growth.

Those are extraordinary numbers, particularly considering the challenging macroeconomic backdrop. But an even more interesting story is unfolding beneath the surface.

The Magnificent Seven are expected to deliver earnings growth of +20.3%, supported by +22.9% revenue growth. However, excluding those seven companies, earnings growth for the rest of the S&P 500 actually increases to +26.0%.

That is a notable development, challenging the widely held assumption that only a handful of mega-cap technology stocks are supporting the market.

Much of that strength is coming from the broader AI infrastructure ecosystem, particularly semiconductor and memory manufacturers, alongside the energy sector. Technology sector earnings are expected to grow +43.3% in Q3, while Energy sector profits are projected to surge +118.1%.

For perspective, an earlier Zacks analysis showed that excluding both Technology and Energy, third-quarter earnings growth for the remaining S&P 500 companies was expected to be just +7.4%. 

The takeaway is that earnings growth remains exceptionally strong, but concentrated. And that concentration creates an important opportunity heading into 2027.

The next phase of this earnings cycle could feature substantially broader participation.

For the fourth quarter, S&P 500 earnings are projected to grow another +27.4%, supported by +12.3% revenue growth, with 15 of the 16 Zacks sectors expected to report positive earnings growth.

Looking further ahead, Zacks projects full-year S&P 500 earnings growth of +28.8% in 2026, followed by another +19.0% in 2027. Even excluding Technology, earnings are expected to increase +11.7% next year, while energy is expected to actually function as a drag on earnings next year.

More importantly, 15 of the 16 Zacks sectors are projected to grow earnings in 2027, with 11 expected to deliver double-digit gains.

The revisions trend is also encouraging. Since the beginning of July, analysts have raised their 2027 earnings estimates across 10 of the 16 Zacks sectors, with upward revisions extending beyond Technology into Finance, Industrials and other industries.

There is reason to believe that process could continue.

If energy prices retreat and interest rates stabilize, companies facing elevated transportation, financing and other operating costs could experience meaningful margin relief. That would support profitability across a much broader portion of the economy.

And importantly, this doesn't require the AI investment boom to end.

My preferred scenario is one in which AI infrastructure spending continues generating exceptional growth, while improving economic conditions allow more traditional industries to contribute meaningfully to the earnings expansion. 

That combination of sustained AI investment and broadening corporate profitability could provide the foundation for a much healthier, more broadly supported bull market in 2027.

3) One of the Market's Most Bullish Seasonal Windows Is Approaching 

The calendar is another reason I am becoming increasingly constructive.

Historically, the months leading up to midterm elections have been among the most challenging periods of the four-year presidential cycle for equity investors. Stocks have frequently experienced heightened volatility and meaningful corrections during this window, with the stretch from late summer through Election Day proving particularly difficult.

This year's market action has followed that historical pattern remarkably closely. Despite strong underlying corporate earnings, stocks have struggled to make sustained progress since early summer, with selling pressure intensifying as the November 3 midterm elections approach.

But what happens afterward is especially interesting. 

Since 1950, the S&P 500 has risen in the 12 months following every midterm election, a perfect 19-for-19 record.

Historical calculations show a median gain of approximately +14.5% over those subsequent 12 months.

The shorter-term record is also encouraging. Research from Schaeffer's Investment Research found that the S&P 500 gained an average of approximately +2.7% between Election Day and year-end during midterm election years, with positive returns about two-thirds of the time.

And the year following a midterm election has historically been the strongest year of the four-year presidential cycle.

There are several possible explanations.

For one, the election removes a major source of uncertainty. Investors can begin assessing actual policy outcomes rather than speculating about potential changes in taxes, regulation and government spending.

Political gridlock can also be viewed favorably, particularly when it reduces the likelihood of disruptive legislative changes.

Of course, historical patterns are not guarantees, and seasonality alone cannot overcome deteriorating earnings or a significant macroeconomic shock.

Nevertheless, the consistency of post-midterm strength is difficult to ignore.

With the election now approaching, the market is entering a period that has historically been exceptionally favorable for equities.

4) Oil and Interest Rates Could Become Powerful Tailwinds

Of all the factors weighing on stocks recently, rising oil prices and interest rates have arguably been the most consequential.

The ongoing conflict involving Iran has introduced a substantial geopolitical risk premium into global energy markets, pushing crude oil above $100 per barrel.

Higher energy costs create multiple problems for the economy. They increase transportation and manufacturing expenses, squeeze household purchasing power and contribute directly to inflation.

Perhaps most importantly for equity investors, higher inflation has complicated the Federal Reserve's policy outlook and contributed to rising Treasury yields.

The 10-year Treasury yield has recently traded above 5%, a level that creates meaningful competition for equities and raises financing costs throughout the economy.

But the relationship works in both directions.

If geopolitical tensions begin easing and oil prices retreat, several of these headwinds could reverse simultaneously.

Lower energy prices would relieve inflationary pressure, potentially allowing interest rate expectations to moderate. Consumers would benefit from lower gasoline prices, while transportation, manufacturing and other energy-intensive businesses could enjoy improving profit margins.

That combination could prove particularly favorable for small-cap stocks, cyclical industries and other market segments that have struggled under the weight of rising borrowing costs.

There is also a possible political catalyst approaching.

With the midterm elections nearly complete, the political incentives surrounding the Middle East conflict could begin changing, potentially creating an opening for renewed diplomatic efforts.

I would not base an investment strategy on predicting a geopolitical resolution. The conflict could just as easily intensify, keeping oil and rates elevated.

However, markets are already reflecting a substantial degree of concern about inflation and higher borrowing costs.

Even a modest improvement in those conditions could be enough to generate a meaningful shift in investor sentiment.

And if the AI spending boom and fiscal support remain intact, the removal of these macroeconomic headwinds could allow the market's underlying bullish forces to reassert themselves. 

5) A New Wave of AI IPOs Could Reignite Risk Appetite 

Finally, one of the more interesting potential catalysts is the approaching wave of major artificial intelligence initial public offerings.

For several years, investors have been able to participate in the AI boom primarily through established technology companies and the businesses supplying the infrastructure behind the industry.

But that could soon change. Anthropic, the developer of Claude, is reportedly preparing for a potential public offering, with speculation pointing toward a possible debut following the midterm elections. Meanwhile, OpenAI is pursuing additional financing and could eventually become another major entrant into the public markets.

These companies represent some of the most closely watched businesses in the world, and their potential listings could become important events for investor sentiment.

One of the largest uncertainties hanging over the AI investment boom is the underlying economics of the companies developing frontier AI models. Investors have relatively little visibility into their revenues, profitability, operating costs and long-term capital requirements. That uncertainty has raised legitimate questions about whether the enormous sums being invested in AI infrastructure will ultimately generate sufficient returns.

Public listings could go a long way toward resolving those concerns.

Greater financial transparency would allow investors to better assess the underlying business models, including revenue growth, margins, customer demand and the economics of developing and operating increasingly sophisticated AI systems.

And while the results could certainly disappoint, many of the recent indications surrounding enterprise adoption, revenue growth and demand for AI services have been encouraging. There is a reasonable possibility that greater transparency could reveal businesses with substantially stronger economics than skeptics currently assume.

That would have implications far beyond the companies themselves.

If investors gain confidence that frontier AI developers can build sustainable, profitable businesses, it would help validate the enormous infrastructure investments being made throughout the industry. That could relieve a major source of uncertainty weighing on semiconductor manufacturers, data center operators, power providers and other AI beneficiaries.

Of course, the opposite outcome is also possible. Disclosures revealing persistent losses, deteriorating unit economics or unsustainable capital requirements could reinforce concerns about an AI investment bubble.

Large IPOs also introduce additional equity supply, potentially absorbing capital that might otherwise flow into existing stocks.

Nevertheless, historically, active and successful IPO markets have tended to accompany periods of strong investor confidence and healthy risk appetite.

If these landmark AI offerings are well received, and the financial disclosures support the increasingly optimistic outlook for AI adoption, they could provide a powerful catalyst for renewed enthusiasm across the entire investment theme. 

What Could Go Wrong? 

Despite these encouraging developments, there are several risks that deserve attention.

The most immediate is the possibility that oil prices and Treasury yields continue climbing, forcing the Federal Reserve to maintain an even more restrictive policy stance.

A further escalation in the Middle East could intensify those pressures and weigh heavily on economic activity.

The other major risk is a meaningful deterioration in AI infrastructure spending.

Much of the market's earnings growth remains tied to enormous capital expenditure commitments from hyperscalers and other technology companies. A material reduction in those spending plans, or evidence that financing conditions are beginning to constrain investment, would directly challenge my underlying bull market thesis.

Finally, earnings expectations are already high. Even strong results may not be enough if corporate guidance begins deteriorating.

These are meaningful concerns, and the market could certainly experience further volatility before a durable advance takes hold. 

The Bull Market's Engines Are Still Running 

The recent market correction has been uncomfortable, but I don't believe the fundamental drivers of the bull market have disappeared.

AI infrastructure investment continues to support exceptional corporate earnings growth, while substantial fiscal deficit spending remains an important source of economic demand.

At the same time, valuations have improved, the earnings outlook remains strong, and the market is approaching one of its most historically favorable seasonal windows.

A potential decline in oil prices, stabilization in interest rates and renewed enthusiasm surrounding major AI IPOs could provide additional catalysts.

Not all five developments need to play out perfectly.

In fact, if even a few of these headwinds begin reversing while the underlying earnings expansion continues, the market could find itself in a substantially more favorable position heading into 2027.

Rather than signaling the end of the bull market, the recent pullback may ultimately prove to be the setup for its next major advance.

Arm Just Dropped 19% in a Month. Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up? ©Alma Grigorita's Images from Canva
Key Takeaways

Arm stock fell 19.8% in the past month (through Tuesday's close). It gave back a 17% jump on Sept. 21 tied to Meta's Muse AI agent, while the Nasdaq 100 slipped 0.5%.

Most of the fall came on days the whole chip sector sold off, and Arm hasn't changed its guidance, so the drop looks like a better entry point than a month ago.

A judge still has to rule whether Qualcomm can stop paying Arm royalties for five years. Qualcomm's payments equal about half of Arm's operating income.

Arm reports its fiscal second quarter on Nov. 4 against revenue guidance of $1.38 billion, with the stock about 32% below the $291 mean analyst target.

Arm Holdings (ARM:NASDAQ) stock is down 19.8% in the past month (through Tuesday's close), while the Nasdaq 100 slipped just 0.5%. It's still up 102% in 2026, but it now sits 51% below its June high.

Most of the damage came on days the whole chip sector sold off. But two of the month's worries are Arm's own, and the bigger one hasn't been settled yet.

The Muse rally didn't last

On Sept. 21, Arm jumped 17% on hopes that Muse, the AI agent from Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ), would lift demand for CPUs, as AI stocks rebounded.

It didn't hold. On Sept. 24, the stock fell 7.9% after reports that SoftBank's Arm stake backs a $25 billion loan facility. Then on Sept. 28, it sank 8.7% as fears about AI safety after a breach hit chip stocks.

By Tuesday, Arm had given back that whole jump and then some, closing about 32% below where it ended Sept. 21.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Arm Holdings, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Arm Holdings' Analyst Ratings

October brought the jury, and more chip selling

Arm fell 6.5% on Oct. 8 as an OpenAI revenue report hit chip stocks. It fell 6.9% on Oct. 16 in a selloff over how AI gets financed, and another 4% on Tuesday after the South Korean neocloud Elice had a weak market debut.

Qualcomm (QCOM:NASDAQ) took its lawsuit against Arm to a jury in Delaware on Oct. 5. On Oct. 13, the jury found Arm breached its license by holding back software patches and tools. It also found that Arm interfered with Qualcomm's dealings with Meta.

The damages? $1 on each of those two claims.

The stock closed about flat that day, then fell 6.8% on Oct. 14.

The judge matters more than the jury

US District Judge Maryellen Noreika still has to rule on whether the breach lets Qualcomm stop paying Arm royalties for five years. Arm argues that clause is unenforceable.

UnitedHealth Soars 11% in a Week After a Beat-and-Raise Quarter: "Discipline and Execution" ©Marta Branco from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

UnitedHealth stock is up 11% in the past week (through Tuesday's close), after a third-quarter beat and a raised 2026 outlook for adjusted EPS of at least $20.50.

The stock lost an early gain on earnings day, then climbed as analysts raised their targets and investors moved out of tech.

The rally can go further, because UnitedHealth's operating margin is still well below its 2024 level and the stock trades below its five-year average multiple.

Members are still leaving, so 2027 guidance, likely early next year, is the next big test.

Wall Street took a day to come around on UnitedHealth Group (UNH:NYSE), then kept buying: shares are up 11% in the past week (through Tuesday's close), as the Nasdaq 100 fell 3.5%.

The market came around in a day

Before the open on Oct. 13, UnitedHealth reported third-quarter adjusted EPS of $4.69, beating the $4.14 expected, and raised its 2026 outlook to at least $20.50 a share. CEO Stephen Hemsley credited "the discipline and execution our teams are bringing to every part of our business."

The stock gave up an early jump that morning. Then the buying started: shares rose 4.7% on Oct. 14 as Goldman Sachs and Piper Sandler lifted their targets, 2.8% on Oct. 15 as investors swapped tech for safer names, and 3% on Tuesday as RBC raised its target to $498 and the rest of managed care rallied.

Margins still have room to run

Revenue slipped to $112.7 billion, but earnings from operations jumped to $6.6 billion from $4.3 billion a year earlier (helped by a $610 million reserve release).

That's an operating margin of about 5.9%, well below the 8.64% it posted in the third quarter of 2024. The yearly margin ran above 8% from fiscal 2021 through fiscal 2024, then fell to 4.8% in fiscal 2025.

Each point of margin UnitedHealth recovers adds about $4.5 billion of yearly operating profit.

The benchmark US stock measures were pointing lower before the open Friday as concerns over artificial intelligence spending continue to weigh on investor sentiment.

The S&P 500 edged down 0.1%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 0.5% in premarket activity, while the Nasdaq 100 slipped 0.1%. Equity markets closed the previous trading session mostly in the red, with the Nasdaq Composite recording its biggest one-day percentage drop since June 5.

Shares of Nvidia (NVDA), Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Tesla (TSLA) were inching higher before the bell after closing the previous session in the red amid concerns over AI-related spending.

Meta Platforms (META), which recently vowed to continue investing aggressively to support its core business and AI initiatives, nudged down 0.6% following a 7% drop at the close of Thursday.

American Express (AXP), SLB (SLB), Infosys (INFY), Rogers Communications (RCI), Booz Allen Hamilton (BAH) and Autoliv (ALV) report their latest financial results before the opening bell, among others.

Treasury yields were moving higher early Friday, with the two-year rate increasing 4.5 basis points to 4.68% and the 10-year rate adding 3.5 basis points to 4.99%.

West Texas Intermediate crude oil gained 1.7% to $101.12 a barrel, while Brent advanced 1.2% to $114.48.

In a social media post on Thursday, President Donald Trump accused Iran of "doing everything they can" to drive up oil prices before the US midterm elections next month. "They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more oil is coming through the (Strait of Hormuz) now than it did even prior to the beginning of the conflict," Trump said.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Thursday that four vessels were struck in the Persian Gulf and three others were hit by mines in the Strait of Hormuz, CNBC reported, citing the state-affiliated Tasnim news agency.

Shares of Moderna (MRNA) fell 5.5% before the bell following an 18% drop at the close of Thursday after leaked data from its experimental cancer vaccine trial fell short of elevated market expectations, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday. Moderna and its partner Merck later said in a statement that their experimental cancer vaccine, intismeran autogene, combined with Keytruda reduced the risk of melanoma recurrence or death by 42% in a phase 3 trial.

Deckers Outdoor (DECK) slipped 8% as the footwear designer and distributor cut its full-year sales outlook. "A promotional US footwear marketplace is driving a softer topline outlook and fueling bear concerns around category saturation/long-term growth durability," Truist said in a Thursday client note about the company.

Friday's economic calendar has the S&P Global's (SPGI) flash purchasing managers' index for October at 9:45 am ET, followed by the final University of Michigan consumer sentiment report for the same month at 10 am. The weekly Baker Hughes oil-and-gas rig count is out at 1 pm.

Spot gold dipped 0.5% to $4,038 per troy ounce, while bitcoin nudged 0.3% higher to $81,602.

Retail sentiment on Stocktwits remained weak. Sentiment toward the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the S&P 500, trended in 'extremely bearish' territory over the past day. US-Iran Tensions Drive Oil Higher

Oil prices rose again amid escalating geopolitical tensions, with reports suggesting that the U.S. and Israel are considering fresh strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections in November. Tehran has vowed to retaliate against any new attacks, potentially targeting economic and civilian infrastructure, the Wall Street Journal reported.

As of 6 a.m. ET, Brent crude futures expiring December were up 1.1% to $114 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 1.6% % to over $101 per barrel.

The Tech Radar

Meta Platforms (META): Shares dipped 0.6% in early premarket trading on Friday, recovering slightly after falling more than 7% on Thursday, when investors reacted negatively to another increase in the company's annual AI spending forecast and plans to issue new shares to help fund the investment. The sell-off came despite better-than-expected results and a strong forecast, highlighting investor concerns about the scale of AI investments and the prospect of even cash-rich technology companies taking on debt to finance them.

Concerns over mounting debt and broader weakness in the AI sector have weighed on the stock. Despite the premarket gains, CRWV was on track for a third straight week of losses as rising borrowing costs and concerns about slowing AI demand continued to weigh on sentiment.

SK Hynix (SKHY): Shares rose almost 5% in premarket trading on Friday. The stock closed 4.4% higher on Thursday, reversing earlier losses of around 3% after the chipmaker halted its review of potential pre-IPO fundraising and listing options for its U.S. subsidiary, Solidigm. According to CNBC, Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for APAC at investment platform eToro, said the recovery suggested concerns over a potential Solidigm IPO had weighed on investor sentiment.

Trending Stocks

Moderna Inc. (MRNA): Shares fell over 4% in premarket trading on Friday, after Moderna's cancer-vaccine rally hit a setback on Thursday. MRNA is heading for its worst weekly performance in three months, while Mizuho analyst Jared Holz warned that extreme volatility had made the stock a "do-not-trade" for many investors. On Thursday, the shares plunged nearly 18% to close at $202.63, marking their steepest single-day decline in more than two months.

Western Digital Corp. (WDC): The stock was down around 2% in premarket trading despite the company beating fiscal first-quarter earnings expectations. The hard-drive maker delivered stronger profits and an upbeat second-quarter outlook, addressing concerns that the storage boom was losing momentum. However, the upbeat results failed to lift sentiment.

Bloom Energy Corp. (BE): Bloom Energy Corp. (BE): Shares of the fuel cell maker dropped as much as 2% in premarket trading on Friday after plunging nearly 9% on Thursday and extending losses overnight. The sell-off followed its third-quarter results, which raised concerns over capital expenditure and cash flow.

Other tickers trending on Stocktwits at the time of writing included Nokia (NOK), Walmart (WMT) and Charles Schwab (SCHW).

What Else To Watch On Friday

On the economic front, traders will watch for the final University of Michigan consumer sentiment reading.

Meanwhile, American Express Co. (AXP) and Schlumberger Ltd. (SLB) are among the companies scheduled to report earnings before the opening bell.

Investing.com - Futures linked to the main U.S. stock indices are mixed, after tech stocks sank in the prior session on growing jitters over the artificial intelligence trade. Anxieties surround the hunt for the capital needed to fund Silicon Valley's rapid AI buildout. At the same time, fears of intensifying violence in the Middle East keep oil prices elevated, while ructions in French bonds also hit sentiment.

Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list »

1. Futures mixed

U.S. stock futures hovered around both sides of the flatline on Friday. By 03:01 ET (07:01 GMT), the S&P 500 futures contract was mostly unchanged, while Nasdaq 100 futures had risen by 45 points, or 0.2%. The Dow futures contract slipped by 149 points, or 0.3%.

The main averages were broadly lower on Thursday, with the Nasdaq Composite slumping by 2.6% -- the worst day for the tech-heavy index since June.

In a note to clients, analysts at Deutsche Bank said "the wobbles of recent weeks all collided at once."

First, the analysts pointed to stress in French bonds as the country grapples with social unrest and a precarious fiscal position. Yields in French debt climbed sharply, sending the spread between French and German bonds, a key European benchmark, up to its biggest daily widening since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020.

While these moves were part of a "clear risk-off pattern," they did not spark a global selloff in bonds, the analysts noted.

2. AI anxieties rise

Instead, investors actually flocked to the relative safety of U.S. Treasuries, pushing the benchmark 10-year yield back down below 5%. Yields tend to move inversely to bond prices.

Traders were spooked by Meta Platforms' decision to roll out a new class of shares, partially as a strategy to help raise funds for its AI ambitions. Like other Big Tech names, the Instagram-owner has laid out plans to spending hundreds of billions on developing its AI capabilities, but have had to incur mounting debt loads to do so.

With borrowing costs expected to rise in the coming months, tech groups are anticipated to sell stock to underpin the next AI spending round. Fears have abounded that such dilution could dent share prices. Meta's stock price slipped 7%, its largest decline since July.

Further compounding these worries, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC that there is "a scarcity of capital" for the AI buildout, adding "the demand for capital is much greater than the availability." Nvidia shares retreated, as did those of peer Advanced Micro Devices. A tracker of the semiconductor industry shed 6.7%.

Meta Platforms (META) share price eased about 6% on Thursday as investors turned anxious over the Instagram maker's negative cash flow amid elevated capex to fund its AI ambitions.

The social media titan posted negative free cash flow while raising its baseline capital expenditure projections in its quarterly earnings filed after-hours on Wednesday, fueling Wall Street's scrutiny over ballooning technology costs.

Compounding these numbers, the company updated its full-year capital expenditure forecast, raising the floor of its projected spending range from $130 billion up to between $135 billion and $145 billion. These figures highlight an aggressive, capital-heavy strategy as the company races to scale its AI infrastructure.

"When you think about a bubble, you think about building capacity and then hoping the demand comes," Blackstone President Jon Gray told Bloomberg Television after the firm reported its third-quarter results. "With AI, you're building capacity, and you're hoping you can keep up with the demand."

Tesla (TSLA) fell -3.1% after trimming its capex plans. Lam Research fell more than -11 after the chip company delivered disappointing guidance.

Stocks were also undercut by a +2.2% rally in WTI oil prices on Middle East tensions after there were several attacks in the past two days by the Houthi militia on targets in Saudi Arabia, including an oil field, a port, and an airport in Dammam. The US State Department also said Wednesday afternoon that it was evacuating non-essential personnel and families from Saudi Arabia.

The Saudi evacuation sparked some market speculation that the US might be planning a new wave of attacks on Iran and/or the Houthis after the November 3 election. Indeed, the New York Times reported Thursday that the US and Israeli militaries have developed specific plans for renewed military strikes against Iran after the US and Israeli elections, although the report said President Trump has not yet approved those plans. The goal of a new military attack would be to deliver a knockout punch to Iran that would topple the government or at least force Iranian leaders to capitulate to US demands, although that has so far only been a fever dream of US planners.
